questions.rationale: The event-specific charge is the filing's clearest disclosed P&L effect; quantify it from the passages read (charge, total provisions, provision releases, net gross-margin effect, segment offset).
questions.text: If In April 2025 the USG informed NVIDIA that a license is required for export to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and D:5 countries of its H20 integrated circuits and similar circuits; as a result NVIDIA incurred a $4.5 billion charge in Q1 fiscal 2026 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations as demand for H20 products diminished., What direct costs did the April 2025 H20 export license requirement produce for NVIDIA in fiscal year 2026 — the $4.5 billion charge, its effect on gross margin, inventory provisions and releases, and the offset to Compute & Networking segment operating income?

questions.rationale: The filing discloses licensing-relief revenue only in this narrow form; the 15% revenue-share expectation is disclosed as uncodified, so what licensed sales actually realize remains open.
questions.text: If In August 2025 the USG granted licenses allowing NVIDIA to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, and in February 2026 the USG granted a license for small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers, subject to U.S. inspection and a 25% tariff on importation into the United States., How much revenue did NVIDIA realize from licensed H20 and H200 sales under the August 2025 and February 2026 licenses, and under what conditions — including the uncodified 15% USG revenue-share expectation and the 25% tariff on H200s imported through the U.S. inspection process?

questions.rationale: Data-center revenue grew sharply while the restrictions were in place; the filing attributes the growth to Blackwell demand and platform shifts, which distinguishes the H20 loss from overall data-center activity.
questions.text: How did NVIDIA's data-center activity perform during the same fiscal year despite the H20 restrictions — Data Center computing (+59%) and networking (+142%) revenue growth, the Hopper-to-Blackwell transition, and total Compute & Networking results?

conditions.hypothesis: In April 2025 the USG informed NVIDIA that a license is required for export to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and D:5 countries of its H20 integrated circuits and similar circuits; as a result NVIDIA incurred a $4.5 billion charge in Q1 fiscal 2026 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations as demand for H20 products diminished.

In August 2025 the USG granted licenses allowing NVIDIA to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, and in February 2026 the USG granted a license for small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers, subject to U.S. inspection and a 25% tariff on importation into the United States.

As of the end of fiscal year 2026 NVIDIA was effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing market, and the foreclosure helped competitors build larger developer and customer ecosystems challenging NVIDIA worldwide.

The USG announced in May 2025 it would rescind the AI Diffusion IFR and implement a replacement rule whose scope and timing remain uncertain; the Senate passed the GAIN AI Act in the NDAA in October 2025; and China's government publicly questioned whether H20 products have built-in vulnerabilities, which NVIDIA publicly denied.

draft:
The framing is saved. Here's where things stand.

## What I read

I acquired your annual report (NVIDIA's Form 10-K for fiscal year 2026, filed 2026-02-25) and located the H20 material through a targeted search. I then read two passages in full context:

1. **The H20 export-control risk factor** (Product/Regulatory risk section, pages ~26–27): the April 2025 license requirement, the $4.5 billion charge, the August 2025 H20 licenses, the February 2026 H200 license, the "effective foreclosure" statement, the AI Diffusion IFR, and the GAIN AI Act. I also read the **next page** as you asked, which adds the China government's H20 vulnerability questions, the design-out risk for customers outside China, and the warning that export controls may hit networking products.
2. **The MD&A gross-margin passage** (page ~41): the quantitative effects of the H20 charge on fiscal 2026 results, plus the adjacent segment operating-income discussion (read via the search results, which surfaced the Compute & Networking passage).

## What the filing establishes

- **The event and the charge:** In April 2025 the USG informed NVIDIA that a license is required to export H20 integrated circuits (and similar circuits) to China (including Hong Kong and Macau), D:5 countries, or companies headquartered there. NVIDIA incurred a **$4.5 billion charge in Q1 fiscal 2026** for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations as demand diminished.
- **Financial effects:** Total inventory/excess-purchase-obligation provisions were **$7.2 billion in FY2026** (vs. $3.7 billion in FY2025), including that $4.5 billion H20 charge; provision releases were **$1.5 billion** (vs. $689 million). The net gross-margin effect was an **unfavorable 2.6 percentage points**; gross margin fell to **71.1% from 75.0%**, attributed to both the Hopper-to-Blackwell transition and the H20 charge. The charge **partially offset** the increase in Compute & Networking segment operating income.
- **Partial licensing relief:** ~**$60 million in H20 revenue** under the August 2025 licenses; the **15% USG revenue-share expectation is uncodified**. The February 2026 H200 license has produced **no revenue to date**, requires U.S. inspection, and carries a **25% tariff** on importation — and NVIDIA says it may not be able to pass the tariff to customers.
- **Data-center growth despite the loss:** Compute & Networking revenue rose **57% to $130.1 billion**, Data Center computing **+59%** (Blackwell demand) and networking **+142%** (NVLink/GB200/GB300, Ethernet, InfiniBand) — so the filing shows the data-center business grew sharply even while China H20 sales collapsed.
- **Competitive claim (company-asserted):** NVIDIA states it was **"effectively foreclosed"** from China's data-center compute market as of fiscal year-end 2026 and that this foreclosure helped competitors build larger developer/customer ecosystems to challenge it worldwide. This is the company's assertion, not independently verified within the filing.

## What remains open (in the saved framing)

- **q1** — Direct charge and margin effect: quantified above; the framing anchors it to the passages read.
- **q2** — Licensed H20/H200 sales: what the narrow licensing relief actually realizes is unresolved (the 15% share is an expectation, not codified regulation).
- **q3** — Data-center growth despite restrictions: the growth figures and Blackwell attribution.
- **q4** — Competitive foreclosure: what the filing supports for its worldwide-ecosystem claim.
- **q5** — Forward uncertainty: H200 program revenue, tariff pass-through, the pending USG replacement rule after the AI Diffusion IFR rescission, the GAIN AI Act, and China's H20 vulnerability questions.

All five questions cite the two passages I actually read (the H20 risk-factor page and the MD&A gross-margin page). Note the framing carries a limitation: q2's "conditions" wording names the licenses and tariff, but the filing gives no dollar figure for any future H200 revenue — that remains genuinely open.

{"packageId":"research-methods-v2","path":"/agent-skills/research-methods-v2/workbench-framing/SKILL.md","resourceHash":"86b25aca343a3eb91ee4e46322190b25f00f7eb13cb79cd0effb9e0b3ada9816","text":"---
name: workbench-framing
description: Prepare a faithful economic research program when an analyst request leaves the relevant activity, event or interpretation uncertain.
---

# Framing an economic inquiry

Consult this method when moving from an analyst's request to a proposed activity and research questions, especially when an announcement could change the program. Read the [worked cases](examples/worked-cases.md) for ambiguous events and the [documentary distinctions](../references/documentary-method.md) for attribution and dates.

Begin with the activity, actors and economic question the analyst actually supplied. Preserve their explicit refinements. Separate their words from a system hypothesis. An analyst's mention of an announcement does not establish that it changes the workflow.

Use the message date and coverage priority to orient discovery. Compare plausible events by their connection to the requested activity, their observed dates and available supporting passages. Read material that can distinguish those interpretations. A newer result can be less relevant; an older release can still explain an explicitly named event. Never describe an event as the latest found when returned observations contradict that statement.

Acquire a useful observed lead or an analyst-supplied URL with `acquire_document`. Use its reading reference with `search_available_material` for a targeted question or `read_in_context` to read from the beginning. Open a returned search reference to see the surrounding passage, and use the returned continuation when more text matters. Cite the exact displayed passage references in a public basis. A reference that opens a document or a later page is a reading instruction and carries no quotation.

Prepare common questions that remain useful across plausible interpretations. Make only event-dependent questions conditional, naming the unresolved condition and its actual basis. Investigate possible economic consequences as questions rather than adding them to the request's premise.

Continue factual checks while they could change the proposed program. When the remaining work is what the program will investigate, present the useful draft and explain how the readings shaped it. If an unresolved distinction materially changes preparation, ask one focused clarification alongside a system-proposed scope. An open event can coexist with a launchable provisional program.

In January 2025, the USG published the AI Diffusion IFR in the Federal Register. The IFR would have imposed a worldwide licensing requirement on our data center products, such as our H200, GB200 and GB300. The AI Diffusion IFR would have divided the world into three tiers, relegating most countries to “Tier 2” status, and would have created a complex and burdensome scheme for licensing approvals.

In May 2025, the USG announced that it would rescind the AI Diffusion IFR and implement a replacement rule. The scope, timing, and requirements of the forthcoming rule remain uncertain. Given the increasing strategic importance of AI and rising geopolitical tensions, the USG has changed and may again change the export control rules at any time and further subject a wider range of our products to export restrictions and licensing requirements, negatively impacting our business and financial results. In the event of such change, we may be unable to sell our inventory of such products and may be unable to develop replacement products not subject to the licensing requirements.

For example, the USG already imposed license conditions that limit the ability of foreign firms to create and offer as a service large-scale GPU clusters, such as imposing license conditions on the use of products to be exported to certain countries, and may impose additional conditions such as requiring chip tracking and throttling mechanisms that could disable or impair GPUs if certain events, including unauthorized system configuration, use, or location, are detected. Such government mandates in chip designs could introduce system vulnerabilities and expose us to significant risk and potential liability, negatively impact demand for our products, and could have a material impact on our business, operating results, and financial condition. Even if not enacted into binding legislation, draft bills have impacted and may in the future negatively impact our business. For example, following U.S. legislative proposals calling for mandatory features in our chips, China’s government publicly questioned whether our H20 products have built-in vulnerabilities, discouraging customers from purchasing our products. We provided a public response explaining that our GPUs, including H20, do not include such built-in vulnerabilities, and will respond to any follow-up questions we receive.

Open-source foundation models are rapidly growing in popularity with developers worldwide. Any regulatory control or other restriction that limits our ability to provide products and services that support third-party applications and models, including applications built on foundation models originating in China such as DeepSeek, Qwen, or KIMMI, could have a material impact on our business, operating results, and financial condition.

The USG already imposed export controls restricting certain gaming GPUs, and if the USG expands such controls to restrict additional gaming products, it may disrupt a significant portion of our supply and distribution chain and

negatively impact sales of such products to markets outside China, including the U.S. and Europe. In addition, as the performance of the gaming GPUs increases over time, export controls may have a greater impact on our ability to compete in markets subject to those controls. Export controls may disrupt our supply and distribution chain for a substantial portion of our products, which are warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong.

Export controls restricting our ability to sell data center GPUs may also negatively impact demand for our networking products used in servers containing our GPUs. The USG may also impose export controls on our networking products, such as high-speed network interconnects, to limit the ability of downstream parties to create large clusters for frontier model training.

Export controls have and are likely in the future to have a disproportionate impact on NVIDIA and may disadvantage us against certain of our competitors that sell chips that are outside the scope of such control. Export controls have already and may in the future encourage customers outside China and other impacted regions to “design-out” certain U.S. semiconductors from their products to reduce the compliance burden and risk, and to ensure that they are able to serve markets worldwide. Export controls have already encouraged and may in the future encourage overseas governments to request that our customers purchase from our competitors rather than NVIDIA or other U.S. firms, harming our business, market position, and financial results.

As a result, export controls have in the past and may in the future negatively impact demand for our products and services not only in China, but also in other markets, such as Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. Export controls increase the risk of investing in U.S. advanced semiconductor products, because by the time a new product is ready for market, it may be subject to new unilateral export controls restricting its sale, resulting in excess inventory and purchase obligations as we recently experienced with the H20. At the same time, such controls may increase investment in foreign competitors, which would be less likely to be restricted by U.S. controls.

The increasingly complex export controls impose complex and burdensome compliance obligations on our partners, suppliers, and customers. While we seek to strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators, reports of diversion of controlled products, even when unsubstantiated and untrue, may negatively impact our business, relationships with partners and customers, and our reputation. Incorrect allegations that our compliance efforts satisfy the letter but not the “spirit” of the applicable regulations, as well as incorrect allegations that legitimate and appropriate business is using supposed “loopholes” in the export controls may negatively impact our business, relationships with partners and customers, and our reputation.

In addition to export controls, the USG may impose restrictions on the import and sale of products that incorporate technologies developed or manufactured in whole or in part in China. For example, the USG adopted “Connected Vehicle” restrictions on the import and sale of certain automotive products in the United States, which if adopted and interpreted broadly, could impact our ability to develop and supply solutions for our automotive customers. Revenue from sales to customers headquartered outside of the United States accounted for 31% and 41% of total revenue for fiscal years 2026 and 2025, respectively.

Gross Profit and Gross Margin

Gross profit consists of total net revenue less cost of revenue. Cost of revenue consists of the cost of semiconductors, including wafer fabrication, assembly, testing and packaging, board and device costs, manufacturing support costs, including labor and overhead associated with such purchases, final test yield fallout, inventory and warranty provisions, memory and component costs, tariffs, and shipping costs. Cost of revenue also includes acquisition-related intangible amortization expense, costs for license and development and service arrangements, IP-related costs, and stock-based compensation related to personnel associated with manufacturing operations.

Gross margins decreased to 71.1% in fiscal year 2026 from 75.0% in fiscal year 2025 as our business model transitioned from offering Hopper HGX systems to Blackwell full-scale datacenter solutions and a $4.5 billion charge associated with H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026.

Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $7.2 billion and $3.7 billion for fiscal years 2026 and 2025, respectively, including $4.5 billion associated with H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations for the first quarter of fiscal year 2026. Sales of previously reserved inventory and settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a provision release of $1.5 billion and $689 million for fiscal years 2026 and 2025, respectively. The net effect on our gross margin was an unfavorable impact of 2.6% and 2.3% in fiscal years 2026 and 2025, respectively.

Income Taxes

Income tax expense was $21.4 billion and $11.1 billion for fiscal years 2026 and 2025, respectively. Income tax as a percentage of income before income tax was an expense of 15.1% and 13.3% for fiscal years 2026 and 2025, respectively.

The effective tax rate increased primarily due to a lower percentage of tax benefits from stock-based compensation, FDDEI, and U.S. federal research tax credit relative to the increase in income before income tax.

Our effective tax rates for fiscal years 2026 and 2025 were lower than the U.S. federal statutory rate of 21.0% primarily due to tax benefits from FDDEI, stock-based compensation, income earned in jurisdictions that are subject to taxes at rates lower than the U.S. federal statutory tax rate, and the U.S. federal research tax credit.

In July 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) was enacted into law and contains several changes to key U.S. federal income tax laws. We have recognized the tax effects of currently effective OBBBA provisions in our results for fiscal year 2026. We will continue to evaluate the impact of these legislative changes as tax authorities provide additional guidance and interpretation.

As of January 25, 2026, based on recent jurisdictional taxable income and expected future earnings, we concluded certain state deferred tax assets are more likely than not realizable and released $711 million of valuation allowance.

In August 2025 the USG granted licenses allowing NVIDIA to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, and in February 2026 the USG granted a license for small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers, subject to U.S. inspection and a 25% tariff on importation into the United States.

As of the end of fiscal year 2026 NVIDIA was effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing market, and the foreclosure helped competitors build larger developer and customer ecosystems challenging NVIDIA worldwide.

The USG announced in May 2025 it would rescind the AI Diffusion IFR and implement a replacement rule whose scope and timing remain uncertain; the Senate passed the GAIN AI Act in the NDAA in October 2025; and China's government publicly questioned whether H20 products have built-in vulnerabilities, which NVIDIA publicly denied.
